units.translation: not to be loathed: not to be defiled, not to be polluted, things that do not defile, which no one would loathe and be disgusted at. The word is rather tragic.

[a useless conjecture which Triclinius applied to the gloss ἐπ᾿ εὐλαβείᾳ [with caution] on verse 1024 of the Agamemnon, introduced in the Florentine copy (for we rely here only on its authority), with a scholium also added, in which he explains his conjecture: about which it will be said under the word εὐλάβεια [caution].]
where the scholium: ἐβλάπτοντο γὰρ οἱ μυσαροῖς ξυντυγχάνοντες [for those who met with polluted persons were harmed].
Knowing the things outside, you will be unharmed.
Darian - unharmed when he is ruler of the bow for the citizens.
to as many as I came with harmless company,
you came as a suppliant, pure and harmless to the house.
for those who met with polluted persons were harmed
This is not to be beguiled by my mind.

what M has from the first hand should not have been changed into ἀβουλίᾳ [recklessness] or ἀβουλίαις [recklessnesses], which is the correction of the copies, but ἀβουλιᾶν [to be reckless] should be written, which the scholiast read, correctly interpreting it as ὑπὸ τῶν αὐτῷ φίλων ἡδονῶν [by the pleasures dear to him].
overcome by the recklessness of his friends, he begot for himself a fate, recklessness,
by the pleasures dear to him

(in the scholium on Aristophanes Av. 277) if Hermannus correctly corrected the corruptions of the books ἀβρατεύς [delicate] (or ἀκρατους) ὃν σθέ. In Aristophanes, who parodies the words of Aeschylus, is read τίς ποτ᾽ ἔσθ᾽ ὁ μουσόμαντις ἄτοπος ὄρνις ὀριβάτης [who ever is this strange bird, the mountain-roaming prophet of the Muses?]
Who ever is this strange, delicate-walking prophet of the Muses?
who ever is this strange bird, the mountain-roaming prophet of the Muses
Correctly the scholium: αἱ ἐντρυφῶσαι τοῖς δάκρυσιν [those luxuriating in tears].
And the softly lamenting Persian women, longing to see their newly yoked husbands --.
the crowd of delicately living Lydians.

ἀκροπενθεῖς [deeply mourning] M, which Paleius corrected, comparing the note of the scholiast ἐπιμόνως πενθοῦσαι, ὡς δοκεῖν ἁβρύνεσθαι ἐπὶ τῷ (τὸ Μ) πενθεῖν [mourning persistently, so as to seem to luxuriate in mourning]. Thus ἁβρόγοοι Περσίδες [softly lamenting Persian women] are spoken of at v. 541.
mourning persistently, so as to seem to luxuriate in mourning
woven with soft or fine thread
woven with soft or fine thread
Thus Salmasius (on Solinus p. 78) emended for άβροτίμων [of delicate honor]. Another example is in Lycophron 863 ἁβροπήνους πέπλους [softly woven robes].
